claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles form a well-mixed solid solution.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles may contain subtle local compositional variations.
Changing cooling rate and precursor-mixing uniformity modulates local chemical heterogeneity in the nanoparticles.
Local compositional variations or defects create micro-regions with lower cohesive energy in the HEA nanoparticles.
Regions with lower cohesive energy begin melting at lower temperatures than neighboring regions.
The different local melting temperatures produce sequential or staggered premelting.
Sequential local melting causes latent heat to be released in stages.
Sequential local melting broadens the overall melting transition.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting-temperature distribution than single-metal or less chemically complex nanoparticles.
The HEA nanoparticles will show identifiable sequential melting steps associated with distinct low-cohesive-energy regions.
Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles exhibit a single, narrow, sharp melting transition under comparable conditions.
Homogeneous bonding and cohesion are responsible for the narrow melting transition attributed to single-metal nanoparticles.
Simpler bimetallic nanoparticles may lack pronounced sequential melting under the same thermal conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies when particle size, mixing, and cooling conditions permit local compositional heterogeneities to develop.
The mechanism may not apply to particles that are too small or are processed to achieve near-perfect mixing.
A single sharp HEA melting transition indistinguishable from the single-metal controls, despite heterogeneity-promoting processing, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
